questions.prompt: What is a security boundary, as this course defines it?
options: A point in a system where the level of trust changes and a check has to run before a request can proceed
A physical firewall appliance installed between two data centers
The maximum number of API calls an org can make per day
A permission set that grants access to encrypted fields
questions.explain: A security boundary is a decision point where trust changes -- crossing it means a check has to run to confirm access is actually allowed, rather than assumed.
questions.distractorExplain: A firewall is just one possible control implementing one specific boundary (the network/org edge) -- it's an example of a control, not the general definition of what a boundary is, which is why option B is too narrow to be the definition itself.

questions.prompt: A new hire is given a cloned copy of the "System Administrator" profile because it's faster than building a scoped profile, with a plan to "remove permissions later." What problem does this create, beyond the immediate convenience?
options: None -- cloning an existing profile is always the recommended least-privilege pattern
It only becomes a problem if the new hire is later promoted
It creates standing, unused risk, because in practice the planned removal step rarely happens on schedule, leaving unjustified access sitting in the org indefinitely
It automatically triggers a Transaction Security Policy violation
questions.explain: Least privilege treats over-permissioning as a real defect: every unneeded permission is unused risk, and the lesson specifically warns that "grant broad access and remove it later" rarely gets the removal step done on schedule, if at all.

questions.prompt: An org's sales rep profile is scoped to owned/shared Accounts only, a sensitive field is protected by FLS and encryption, and a Transaction Security Policy flags unusual logins. A phishing attack still steals the rep's password and the attacker logs in. What does defense in depth say about the outcome?
options: The attacker automatically gains full access to every record and field in the org, since the login layer failed
Nothing can be done once a password is phished, regardless of other controls

The authorization, field-level, and monitoring layers each independently limit the damage, because defense in depth assumes the login layer will eventually fail and designs the other layers to not depend on it holding
The incident proves defense in depth does not work in practice
questions.explain: This is the lesson's worked example: one layer failing (phished login) doesn't mean total breach, because the other independent layers -- scoped authorization, field-level protection, and monitoring/response -- each do their own, narrower job regardless of the login layer's failure.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the standard Salesforce feature that records configuration changes made in Setup -- such as a profile being edited or a user being deactivated -- without tracking record-level field value changes, is called the ________.
questions.explain: Setup Audit Trail records administrative/configuration changes made in Setup; it's a separate feature from Field History Tracking, which tracks changes to a record's actual field values over time.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the STRIDE threat-modeling framework as taught in this course.
options: STRIDE stands for Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege
Going through all six STRIDE categories deliberately helps surface threats that a single "is this secure?" conversation might miss
STRIDE guarantees that every possible threat will be found as long as all six letters are checked
A design can be airtight against one STRIDE category, like information disclosure, while still having a real gap in a different category, like repudiation
STRIDE should only ever be applied to inbound integrations, never to public-facing forms
questions.explain: STRIDE's six categories are Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege. Going through all six surfaces different threats than a single open-ended question would, precisely because a design can be solid in one category and still have a real gap in another. STRIDE is a systematic checklist, not a guarantee of completeness, and this course applied it to both an integration and a public donation form.

questions.prompt: Match each security boundary to the control that primarily guards it.
right: Field-Level Security and Shield Platform Encryption
Login IP ranges, trusted IP ranges, and multi-factor authentication
Org-Wide Defaults, role hierarchy, and sharing rules
Profile and permission set object permissions
questions.explain: The org boundary is guarded by network/identity controls (login IP, MFA). The object/CRUD boundary is guarded by profile/permission set object permissions. The record-sharing boundary is guarded by OWD, role hierarchy, and sharing rules. The innermost field-level boundary is guarded by FLS and Shield Platform Encryption.

questions.prompt: A company encrypts its SSN field at rest with strong encryption, but Field-Level Security leaves it visible to every Service Agent profile, and nothing monitors who views or exports it. What does this configuration actually protect against, and what does it leave uncovered?
options: It protects against everything, since strong encryption is the only control that matters

It protects against someone bypassing the application entirely (a stolen disk, a raw backup), but does not restrict which authenticated, authorized users can see the field through the normal app, and leaves unusual access undetected
It leaves the data completely unprotected, since encryption without monitoring provides zero benefit
It fully restricts which Service Agents can see the field, in addition to protecting stored data
questions.explain: Encryption protects confidentiality against someone bypassing the application entirely; it does nothing to restrict a legitimately authorized user viewing the field through the normal UI, and with no monitoring in place, unusual legitimate-looking access also goes undetected -- both the authorization (FLS) and monitoring layers are separately needed to close this gap.

questions.prompt: What is the key functional difference between Shield Platform Encryption's probabilistic and deterministic encryption schemes?
options: Probabilistic encryption produces different ciphertext for the same plaintext each time and cannot generally be filtered on; deterministic encryption always produces the same ciphertext for the same plaintext, which enables exact-match filtering
Deterministic encryption is only available on Classic Encryption, not Shield Platform Encryption
Probabilistic encryption is required for every standard field, with no exceptions
There is no real functional difference between the two schemes
questions.explain: Probabilistic encryption's randomness makes identical plaintext produce different ciphertext each time, which blocks filtering; deterministic encryption's consistency enables exact-match filtering, at the cost of being more exposed to certain pattern-based inference.
questions.distractorExplain: Deterministic encryption is a scheme offered specifically within Shield Platform Encryption, not Classic Encryption -- Classic Encryption is the older, far more limited capability that predates this scheme choice entirely.

questions.prompt: A law firm wants to encrypt a long free-text `Case_Notes__c` field that is never searched or filtered on. Which encryption scheme best fits this field, and why?
options: Deterministic, because every encrypted field should default to the filterable option

Probabilistic, because the field is never queried or filtered, so there's no need to accept deterministic encryption's greater exposure to pattern-based inference just to gain filtering capability it doesn't need
Classic Encryption, because it is the modern recommended option for new designs
Neither scheme -- long text fields can never be encrypted under any circumstances
questions.explain: Since the field is never filtered or searched, there's no reason to accept deterministic encryption's tradeoff (greater exposure to pattern-based inference in exchange for filterability) -- probabilistic encryption is the better fit precisely because the filtering capability isn't needed.

questions.prompt: A security team wants to automatically block any single user from exporting more than a set number of records within an hour, the instant the threshold is crossed. Which Event Monitoring family tool is actually capable of this, and why not the others?
options: Event Log Files, because they contain the most comprehensive historical event data
Event Log Objects, because they can be queried through the standard API
Transaction Security Policies, because unlike the purely observational tools, they can take a real-time action (like blocking a transaction) when a policy's conditions are met
Setup Audit Trail, because it records every administrative change
questions.explain: Event Log Files and Event Log Objects are observational and not instantaneous; Setup Audit Trail tracks configuration changes, not data exports. Only Transaction Security Policies can actually act -- blocking, challenging, or freezing -- the instant a real-time condition is met.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Apex sharing and CRUD/field-level security (FLS) enforcement.
options: `with sharing` enforces the running user's record-sharing rules inside that class's queries and DML
Apex automatically enforces CRUD and field-level security by default, with no extra code required
`inherited sharing` runs a class as with sharing at entry points, but defers to without sharing only when called from an already-without-sharing context
`Security.stripInaccessible()` can be used to strip fields a user shouldn't see or write before they're exposed or committed
SOQL injection is prevented by concatenating user input directly into the query string
questions.explain: `with sharing` enforces record-sharing rules specifically. Apex does NOT enforce CRUD/FLS by default -- it runs in system context, so that must be added deliberately (WITH USER_MODE, WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED, explicit checks, or stripInaccessible()). `inherited sharing` gives a safe with-sharing default at entry points while still respecting an already-without-sharing caller. SOQL injection is prevented by using bind variables, not by concatenating raw input -- concatenation is the vulnerability, not the fix.

questions.prompt: A Connected App for a new integration requests `full` OAuth scope when the integration only needs to read a handful of fields on one object. What should an architect reviewing this request conclude?
options: This is fine, since `full` scope is required for any integration to function at all

This is a least-privilege violation at the integration layer -- the Connected App should be scoped to request only what the integration's actual job requires, such as `api` with a narrowly scoped integration user
OAuth scopes have no bearing on integration security and can be ignored during review
The integration user's profile is irrelevant as long as the OAuth scope is correct
questions.explain: Requesting broader access than the integration's actual job requires is a least-privilege violation at the integration layer, the same reasoning Lesson 2 applies to human profiles -- and the integration user's own profile/permission sets still matter independently of the Connected App's scope.

questions.prompt: Match each integration scenario to the Named Credential authentication model that best fits it.
left: A nightly batch job syncing records with no individual human session involved
A feature where the external system must know specifically which individual employee is acting, for its own audit trail
questions.explain: Named Principal fits service-account-style automation like a batch job, since there's no individual session to attribute. Per-User fits cases where the external system needs individual-level accountability, since each user authenticates with their own credentials.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the OAuth scope that lets an integration keep working without the user present, by exchanging a refresh token for a new access token, is called ________.
questions.explain: The `refresh_token` scope lets an integration obtain a refresh token so it can continue operating after the user's session ends, rather than requiring the user to be present for every access token renewal.

questions.prompt: An auditor asks whether least-privilege access reviews actually happened every quarter for the past year. Why does a current, well-written design document describing the access model not answer this question on its own?
options: Documentation explains what was designed and why; it does not prove a control actually operated on a specific occasion or continuously -- that requires evidence captured at the time, which is a separate thing
Design documents are never useful for any audit purpose
Auditors are only interested in Health Check scores, never in documentation
This question can only be answered by a Transaction Security Policy log
questions.explain: Documentation shows intent and design rationale; it doesn't prove operation. Proving reviews actually happened every quarter requires evidence -- dated artifacts captured at the time -- which is a categorically different thing from a design document.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a SOC 2 Type ________ report requires evidence that controls operated consistently over an observation period (often 6-12 months), as opposed to a single point-in-time assessment.
questions.explain: A SOC 2 Type II report requires evidence spanning an observation period, showing a control operated consistently over time -- a Type I report, by contrast, is a single point-in-time assessment.

questions.prompt: A Transaction Security Policy freezes a compromised user's account the moment unusual activity is detected. The investigation later finds the credential was phished three days earlier. What would eradication require, beyond this containment step?
options: Nothing further -- freezing the account fully resolves the incident on its own
Permanently deleting the user's account and all related records

Addressing the actual root cause once understood -- for example, resetting the compromised credential for good and reviewing whether any access the attacker gained during those three days needs to be remediated
Simply unfreezing the account once the immediate alert stops
questions.explain: Freezing the account is containment -- an immediate, temporary damage-limiting step. Eradication is the deeper fix: addressing the actual root cause (the compromised credential, and whatever the attacker touched in the interim) so the incident doesn't simply recur once the temporary containment measure is lifted.

questions.prompt: Put the six phases of the incident response lifecycle in the correct order.
questions.explain: The lifecycle runs: Preparation (before anything happens), Detection and analysis (recognizing and understanding the incident), Containment (limiting damage immediately), Eradication (removing the root cause), Recovery (restoring normal operation), and Lessons learned (feeding findings back into the review process).

questions.prompt: Match each incident response phase to the Salesforce-specific tool or practice that most directly supports it.
right: Freezing the user or ending the session via a Transaction Security Policy
Review board process and a current, accurate data flow diagram, established before any incident occurs
Event Log Files/Objects and Real-Time Event Monitoring
questions.explain: Preparation relies on things set up in advance, like the review board process and an accurate data flow diagram. Detection and analysis draws on Event Monitoring tools to recognize and understand what's happening. Containment uses real-time actions like a Transaction Security Policy freezing a user or ending a session.

questions.prompt: Following this course's seven-step forward-design method, a new client-facing portal is being designed. After naming boundaries and applying least privilege, what should happen next, before the design is considered complete?
options: The design is already complete once boundaries and least privilege are addressed -- no further steps are needed

Add independent depth layers, run a STRIDE threat pass on sensitive surfaces, make explicit encryption/monitoring decisions, wrap the design in a review and evidence plan, and sanity-check it against incident response -- each step surfaces something the previous ones don't
Skip directly to writing the incident response plan, since it's the most important step
Only Health Check needs to be run once least privilege is addressed
questions.explain: The method's remaining steps -- depth, threat modeling, encryption/monitoring decisions, governance wrapping, and an incident-response sanity check -- each surface a different kind of gap that boundaries and least privilege alone don't catch, which is exactly why the method treats them as separate, deliberate steps rather than skipping to just one.
